notes.definition: A chemical bond is a strong force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together. There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic, and all of them involve the outer shell electrons of the atoms.
explanation: Atoms join together by chemical bonds. The type of bond depends on the type of elements involved. In ionic bonding the particles are oppositely charged ions. Ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals, such as sodium chloride (NaCl) or magnesium oxide (MgO). In covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements, such as hydrogen (H₂) and chlorine (Cl₂), and in compounds of non-metals, such as water (H₂O) and carbon dioxide (CO₂).

In metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons. Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements, such as copper and iron, and in alloys, such as brass and steel. The outer shell electrons are not tied to one atom but are free to move through the whole structure. A useful way to decide the bond type is to look at where the elements are in the periodic table: metals are on the left and in the middle, non-metals are on the right.

When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom, electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion. The non-metal atom gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion. Opposite charges attract, and this strong electrostatic attraction between the ions is the ionic bond. For example, a sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

When two non-metal atoms bond, neither atom gives up electrons easily, so instead they share pairs of electrons. Each shared pair is one covalent bond. The shared electrons are attracted to the nuclei of both atoms, which holds the atoms together. Covalent bonds are strong. Both atoms usually end up with a full outer shell, like a noble gas. In metals, each atom gives up its outer shell electrons to a shared pool, leaving positive metal ions. The attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is the metallic bond.

All three types of bond are strong, and all three involve electrons. The difference is what happens to the outer shell electrons: they are transferred (ionic), shared in pairs between two atoms (covalent) or shared throughout the structure (metallic). The type of bonding a substance has explains many of its properties, such as its melting point and whether it conducts electricity, which you will meet in later subtopics.
keyFacts: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic.
Ionic bonding: between a metal and a non-metal; the particles are oppositely charged ions.
Covalent bonding: between non-metals (elements or compounds); atoms share pairs of electrons.
Metallic bonding: in metallic elements and alloys; atoms share delocalised electrons.
In ionic bonding electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom.
Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.
Each shared pair of electrons is one covalent bond.
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole metal structure.
Bonding involves the electrons in the outer shell of atoms.

keyTerms.definition: A strong force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together in an element or compound.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge, formed when electrons are lost or gained.
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal.
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
The strong attraction between positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons shared between them.
Electrons that are not associated with a particular atom or bond and are free to move through a structure.
The force of attraction between opposite electric charges.
A mixture of a metal with at least one other element, usually another metal; alloys have metallic bonding.

workedExamples.title: Deciding the type of bonding
workedExamples.question: State the type of bonding in: (a) potassium bromide, KBr; (b) ammonia, NH₃; (c) magnesium, Mg; (d) sulfur dioxide, SO₂.
steps: Decide whether each element is a metal or a non-metal using the periodic table.
(a) Potassium is a metal and bromine is a non-metal: metal + non-metal gives ionic bonding.
(b) Nitrogen and hydrogen are both non-metals: covalent bonding.
(c) Magnesium is a metallic element on its own: metallic bonding.
(d) Sulfur and oxygen are both non-metals: covalent bonding.

workedExamples.title: What happens to the electrons
workedExamples.question: Calcium reacts with chlorine to form calcium chloride. Describe what happens to the electrons when the bond forms and name the type of bond.
steps: Calcium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so the bonding is ionic.
Calcium atoms have 2 electrons in their outer shell; these are transferred to chlorine atoms.
Each chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons and gains 1 electron, so one calcium atom transfers electrons to two chlorine atoms.
Calcium becomes a positive ion (Ca²⁺) and each chlorine becomes a negative ion (Cl⁻).
The oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly.
workedExamples.answer: Electrons are transferred from calcium to chlorine, forming Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds (electrostatic attraction).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think ionic bonds involve sharing electrons.
misconceptions.right: In ionic bonding electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom; sharing happens in covalent bonding.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think covalent bonds are weak because substances like water have low boiling points.
misconceptions.right: Covalent bonds are strong. Small molecules have low boiling points because the forces between molecules are weak, not the bonds inside them.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metallic bonding is the same as ionic bonding because metals form positive ions.
misconceptions.right: In a metal there are no negative ions: the positive metal ions are held together by attraction to a sea of delocalised electrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals gain electrons to form ions.
misconceptions.right: Metal atoms lose their outer shell electrons to form positive ions; non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a compound containing hydrogen must be ionic because H⁺ ions exist.
misconceptions.right: Compounds made only of non-metals, such as HCl and CH₄, are covalent.

realWorld: Table salt (sodium chloride) is an ionic compound; its bonding explains why it forms hard crystals.
Copper wiring relies on metallic bonding: the delocalised electrons carry electric current.
Oxygen (O₂) and nitrogen (N₂) in the air are covalently bonded molecules.
Alloys such as steel and brass are made by mixing metals, and they are still held together by metallic bonding.
examTips: Start by classifying each element as a metal or a non-metal: metal + non-metal = ionic, non-metals only = covalent, metal only (or an alloy) = metallic.
Use precise wording: ionic bonds involve electrons being transferred; covalent bonds are shared pairs of electrons; metallic bonds involve delocalised electrons.
Say which way electrons move: from the metal to the non-metal. Writing that the non-metal 'gives' electrons loses the mark.
Never call the particles in an ionic compound 'molecules' or 'atoms': they are ions.
summary: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic.
Ionic bonding: metal + non-metal, electrons transferred, oppositely charged ions attract.
Covalent bonding: non-metals, atoms share pairs of electrons.
Metallic bonding: metals and alloys, atoms share delocalised electrons.
Metal atoms lose electrons (positive ions); non-metal atoms gain electrons (negative ions).

questions.question: How many types of strong chemical bond are there in the AQA specification?
markScheme: 1 mark: Three
questions.explanation: There are three: ionic, covalent and metallic. Intermolecular forces are not chemical bonds.

questions.question: Which type of bonding is found in sodium chloride?
markScheme: 1 mark: Ionic
questions.explanation: Sodium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so the bonding is ionic. Covalent bonding is between non-metals only.

questions.question: Which substance has covalent bonding?
markScheme: 1 mark: Methane
questions.explanation: Methane (CH₄) contains only the non-metals carbon and hydrogen, so it is covalent. Magnesium oxide and potassium iodide are metal + non-metal (ionic); copper is metallic.

questions.question: In metallic bonding, the atoms share:
options: pairs of electrons between two atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: In metals the outer shell electrons are delocalised and shared through the whole structure. Shared pairs between two atoms describe covalent bonding.

questions.question: What happens when a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom?
options: The metal atom gains electrons from the non-metal atom.
The atoms share a pair of electrons.
The metal atom transfers outer shell electrons to the non-metal atom.
Protons are transferred from the non-metal to the metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: The metal atom transfers outer shell electrons to the non-metal atom.
questions.explanation: Metal atoms lose outer shell electrons, which are transferred to the non-metal atom. Protons are never transferred in chemical reactions; sharing is covalent.

questions.question: Which row correctly describes the ions formed when lithium reacts with fluorine?
markScheme: 1 mark: Li⁺ and F⁻
questions.explanation: Lithium (a metal) loses one electron to form Li⁺; fluorine (a non-metal) gains one electron to form F⁻. Metals always form positive ions.

questions.question: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. What type of bonding is in brass?
options: A mixture of ionic and covalent
markScheme: 1 mark: Metallic
questions.explanation: Alloys of metals are held together by metallic bonding: positive ions and delocalised electrons. There is no non-metal to form ionic or covalent bonds.

questions.question: Which pair of elements would form a covalent compound?
markScheme: 1 mark: Carbon and chlorine
questions.explanation: Carbon and chlorine are both non-metals, so they share electrons (CCl₄). The other pairs all contain a metal, so they form ionic compounds.

questions.question: Which statement about all three types of strong chemical bond is correct?
options: They all involve the transfer of electrons.
They all involve electrons from the outer shells of atoms.
They all form between a metal and a non-metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: They all involve electrons from the outer shells of atoms.
questions.explanation: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding all involve outer shell electrons. Only ionic bonding involves transfer; covalent bonding does not produce ions.

questions.question: A substance is made of particles held together by strong attraction between positive ions and electrons that move freely through the structure. The substance could be:
markScheme: 1 mark: aluminium
questions.explanation: Positive ions plus free (delocalised) electrons describes metallic bonding, so the substance is a metal: aluminium. Aluminium oxide is ionic; the others are covalent.

questions.question:
Name the type of bonding in:
(a) water, H₂O
(b) iron, Fe
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) covalent
1 mark: (b) metallic
questions.explanation: Water contains only non-metals, so the atoms share pairs of electrons (covalent). Iron is a metallic element, so it has metallic bonding.

questions.question: State what a covalent bond is.
markScheme: 1 mark: a shared pair of electrons (between two atoms)
questions.explanation: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms, usually non-metal atoms.

questions.question: Describe the charges on the ions formed by metal atoms and by non-metal atoms in ionic bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark: metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions
1 mark: non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions
questions.explanation: Losing negatively charged electrons leaves the metal ion with more protons than electrons, so it is positive. Gaining electrons makes the non-metal ion negative.

questions.question: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Describe what happens to the electrons when magnesium oxide forms.
markScheme: 1 mark: (two) electrons are transferred from magnesium (atom) to oxygen (atom)
1 mark: forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions / positive magnesium ion and negative oxide ion
questions.explanation: Magnesium is in Group 2 and loses its 2 outer electrons; oxygen is in Group 6 and gains 2 electrons. Both ions then have a full outer shell.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by delocalised electrons in a metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: outer shell electrons (of the metal atoms)
1 mark: are free to move through the whole structure / not tied to any one atom
questions.explanation: In a metal the outer shell electrons leave their atoms and move freely throughout the structure, shared by all the positive ions.

questions.question:
Complete the sentences.
In ionic bonding, the particles are ____. In covalent bonding, the particles are atoms which ____. In metallic bonding, the particles are atoms which share ____ electrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: oppositely charged ions
1 mark: share pairs of electrons
1 mark: delocalised
questions.explanation: These three sentences summarise the spec statement for 4.2.1.1. 'Ions' alone is acceptable for the first mark only if the idea of opposite charges is clear.

questions.question: Classify each substance as having ionic, covalent or metallic bonding: (a) CaCl₂ (b) NH₃ (c) Zn (d) CO
markScheme: 2 marks: all four correct: (a) ionic (b) covalent (c) metallic (d) covalent
1 mark: two or three correct
questions.explanation: Calcium is a metal with chlorine (ionic). NH₃ and CO contain only non-metals (covalent). Zinc on its own is metallic.

questions.question: A student says: 'In sodium chloride the sodium and chlorine atoms share electrons, so it is held together by covalent bonds.' Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium is a metal (and chlorine a non-metal) so the bonding is ionic
1 mark: an electron is transferred from sodium to chlorine (not shared)
1 mark: forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by (electrostatic) attraction between opposite charges
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding only happens between non-metals. Sodium loses its single outer electron to chlorine, forming ions which attract each other.

questions.question: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) dissolves in water to form H⁺ ions. Explain why HCl gas is described as having covalent bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals
1 mark: the atoms share a pair of electrons (so HCl gas is made of molecules, not ions)
questions.explanation: The type of bonding depends on the elements: two non-metals share electrons. Ions only form later, when HCl reacts with water.

questions.question: Suggest why non-metal atoms share electrons with each other rather than transferring them.
acceptedAnswers: both get a full outer shell by sharing
markScheme: 1 mark: both atoms need to gain electrons (to get a full outer shell) / neither atom readily loses electrons
1 mark: by sharing pairs of electrons both atoms gain a full outer shell
questions.explanation: Non-metal atoms have nearly full outer shells, so neither wants to lose electrons. Sharing lets both count the shared electrons towards a full shell.

questions.question: Name the type of bonding found in alloys such as steel.
markScheme: 1 mark: metallic
questions.explanation: Alloys are mixtures of metals (or a metal with small amounts of another element), and they keep metallic bonding.

questions.question: Give two ways in which ionic bonding and metallic bonding are similar.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: both are strong; both contain positive (metal) ions; both involve the outer shell electrons of metal atoms; both involve electrostatic attraction between opposite charges
questions.explanation: Both have positive metal ions held by attraction to negative charge: in ionic compounds the negative charge is on non-metal ions; in metals it is the delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Element X is in Group 1 and element Y is in Group 7. Element Z is in Group 6. Which compound would contain covalent bonds?
options: a compound of Y and Z
a compound of X and Z
markScheme: 1 mark: a compound of Y and Z
questions.explanation: Group 1 elements are metals, so X with Y or Z gives ionic compounds. Y (Group 7) and Z (Group 6) are both non-metals, so their compound is covalent, for example Cl₂O.

questions.question: Compare how electrons are involved in ionic bonding and in covalent bonding. Give one example of a substance with each type of bonding.
markScheme: Indicative content: ionic: between metal and non-metal; outer shell electrons transferred from metal atom to non-metal atom; metal forms positive ion, non-metal forms negative ion; oppositely charged ions attract (electrostatic attraction); example NaCl or MgO. Covalent: between non-metal atoms; atoms share pairs of electrons; each shared pair is one bond; no ions formed; example H₂O, CH₄, Cl₂.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of transfer versus sharing, with ions formed in ionic but not covalent bonding, and a correct example of each
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements such as 'ionic transfers, covalent shares', or one correct example
questions.explanation: The key contrast is transfer (forming charged ions) versus sharing (forming molecules or giant covalent structures). Examples must match: a metal + non-metal for ionic, non-metals only for covalent.

questions.question:
Sodium, chlorine and sodium chloride each have a different type of bonding.
Describe the bonding in each substance. In your answer refer to the particles involved and what happens to the electrons.
markScheme: Indicative content: sodium: metallic bonding; giant structure of positive sodium ions; outer shell electron of each atom is delocalised; free to move through the whole structure; strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons. Chlorine: covalent bonding; non-metal atoms; two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons; forming Cl₂ molecules; each atom gets a full outer shell. Sodium chloride: ionic bonding; metal and non-metal; sodium transfers one electron to chlorine; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three types correctly named and described with the correct particles (ions, atoms/molecules, ions) and correct electron behaviour (delocalised, shared pair, transferred)
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two bond types correctly described, or all three named with limited description of the electrons
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two bond types named, with little or confused description
questions.explanation: This tests the whole of 4.2.1.1. The best answers name the particles (positive ions and delocalised electrons; atoms sharing a pair; oppositely charged ions) and describe the electron movement in each.

questions.question: Explain how you can use the position of elements in the periodic table to predict the type of bonding in a substance. Use examples.
markScheme: Indicative content: metals are on the left and in the centre; non-metals on the right; metal + non-metal: ionic, e.g. KCl, MgO; non-metals only: covalent, e.g. H₂O, NH₃, Cl₂; metal element or alloy: metallic, e.g. Cu, Fe, steel; explanation: metals lose electrons easily, non-metals gain or share electrons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct rule for all three types with appropriate examples and some reasoning about electrons
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two rules stated, perhaps with an example
questions.explanation: The location in the periodic table tells you whether an element is a metal or non-metal, which decides the bond type.
